ideas.title: Surprisal-Based Difficulty Estimation as a Cross-Benchmark Item Calibration Tool

original_idea.body:
# Surprisal-Based Difficulty Estimation as a Cross-Benchmark Item Calibration Tool

**Problem:** Safety benchmark item difficulty is typically estimated empirically (proportion of models that pass), which requires running many models on every item. Psycholinguistic surprisal theory offers a model-free way to estimate item difficulty from the linguistic properties of the text, enabling rapid calibration of new items before deployment.

**Direction:** Import surprisal theory from psycholinguistics: compute surprisal (negative log probability of each token in an item) as a proxy for item complexity. Use this as an a priori difficulty estimate and test its correlation with empirical item difficulty from IRT-calibrated safety benchmarks. Extend to compute 'semantic surprisal' using sentence embedding distances. Validate by splitting items into tertiles by surprisal and checking whether empirical difficulty monotonically increases. Implement in R with a pre-trained language model API (read-only).

**Why it matters:** Surprisal-based item difficulty estimation would allow benchmark designers to calibrate item difficulty without running full model evaluations—dramatically accelerating benchmark development and enabling rapid generation of calibrated new items to counter benchmark saturation.

**Relevant context:** Psycholinguistics literature shows LM surprisal outperforms cloze probability as a difficulty predictor (arXiv 2601.09886, PLOS Comput Biol 2024). arXiv IRT-LLM papers calibrate empirical difficulty. This is a validation study correlating two measures in R—no model training, just API calls for probability scores.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Vague impact: faster benchmark calibration is useful but the chain to reducing catastrophic AI risk is diffuse. It accelerates benchmark development but does not target a specific risk mechanism.

low_compute.reasoning: Mostly statistical analysis in R, but requires API calls to compute surprisal values for benchmark items. This is light but not zero compute.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires understanding psycholinguistic surprisal theory, computing token-level probabilities via API, and correlating with IRT difficulty estimates. The validation methodology is straightforward but the conceptual bridge between surprisal and item difficulty is non-trivial.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused first deliverable: compute surprisal for items in one benchmark, correlate with empirical IRT difficulty, report correlation. Clear and self-contained.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Addresses AI safety benchmark design but the core methodology (surprisal-based difficulty estimation) is a general psycholinguistic technique; the safety framing is present but the scope is broad.

ideas.title: The Population Assumption Problem: Formalizing Non-Populational IRT for AI Safety Evaluation

original_idea.body:
# The Population Assumption Problem: Formalizing Non-Populational IRT for AI Safety Evaluation

**Problem:** IRT assumes persons are sampled from a well-defined population with a specified ability distribution (typically normal). AI models are not randomly sampled — they are selected by researchers, released by labs, and include survivors of model selection processes. Recent work has proposed 'non-populational' IRT where a single model's ability is estimated from its own response pattern, independent of the model population. This approach has not been applied to safety benchmarks or compared to standard IRT.

**Direction:** Apply both standard IRT (assuming a normal model-ability population) and non-populational IRT (ability estimated from single-model response patterns without population assumption) to the same safety benchmark data. Compare: (1) ability estimates from each approach and their rank-order correlation, (2) item parameter estimates under each assumption, (3) confidence intervals and their coverage probabilities via bootstrap. Assess when the approaches diverge and what this divergence implies for safety score interpretation.

**Why it matters:** If non-populational IRT produces substantially different safety rankings from standard IRT, the assumption violation is practically significant. This paper would establish when and why the population assumption matters for AI evaluation — a foundational methodological contribution that applies across all IRT-based AI evaluation, not just safety.

**Relevant context:** The 'General Scales Unlock AI Evaluation' paper (arXiv:2503.06378) develops non-populational IRT for AI. The 'Stop Evaluating AI with Human Tests' paper (arXiv:2507.23009) explicitly addresses assumption violations. Standard IRT violation effects are documented in the IRT literature. The mirt package implements standard IRT for comparison.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Vague impact: the population assumption problem is a foundational methodological concern, but the link to reducing catastrophic risk is indirect and theoretical. The contribution is to measurement theory, not safety outcomes.

low_compute.reasoning: IRT analysis in R comparing two approaches on existing data. CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires advanced understanding of IRT assumptions, non-populational IRT (a niche topic), and bootstrap methods. Advanced difficulty.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused: compare standard vs non-populational IRT on same data. Clear deliverable but requires implementing non-standard IRT.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Relevant to AI safety evaluation methodology but the scope is broad and foundational; the safety connection is indirect via improved measurement assumptions.

ideas.title: MIRT Subscale Structure of a Safety Benchmark: Testing Unidimensionality vs. Multidimensionality

original_idea.body:
# MIRT Subscale Structure of a Safety Benchmark: Testing Unidimensionality vs. Multidimensionality

**Problem:** Open problem 6 in measurement-theoretic AI evaluation is whether unidimensional IRT is sufficient or whether MIRT is needed. This is empirically unresolved for any safety benchmark. If safety performance is multidimensional (e.g., separate dimensions for refusal, factual accuracy, bias avoidance), collapsing to a single score loses critical information.

**Direction:** Use a safety benchmark with clear thematic subtasks (e.g., AIR-Bench 2024 with its four risk domains: system/operational risks, content safety, societal risks, legal risks). Extract item-level model responses from published data. In R (mirt package), fit: (1) one-factor unidimensional model, (2) 4-factor correlated MIRT model aligned with AIR-Bench categories, (3) bifactor model. Compare using AIC/BIC. Compute dimensionality indices (DETECT, explained common variance). Report whether safety performance on AIR-Bench is best characterized as one ability or four correlated abilities.

**Why it matters:** The dimensionality question determines whether a single safety score is scientifically defensible. If safety is multidimensional, claiming a model is 'safe overall' based on a composite score is psychometrically invalid. This analysis would provide the first MIRT-based empirical answer to open problem 6 for a safety-specific benchmark.

**Relevant context:** Open problem 6 (MIRT vs. unidimensional IRT); MEDIRT framework for medical LLMs (arxiv:2509.24186) uses 11 unidimensional models per topic; AIR-Bench 2024 has 4 risk domains; mirt R package supports MIRT; Open LLM Leaderboard scores available.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: if safety is multidimensional but scored unidimensionally, models may appear safe overall while being dangerous on specific dimensions. Names the specific mechanism but the link to catastrophic risk is mediated by governance decisions.

low_compute.reasoning: MIRT modeling in R on existing data. No model inference needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: MIRT and bifactor modeling are advanced psychometric techniques. Requires understanding factor structures, model comparison, DETECT statistic, and ECV. This is substantially beyond beginner level even with mentor guidance.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused on one benchmark (AIR-Bench) which helps scope, but requires fitting three model types and computing multiple dimensionality indices. Could be scoped to just unidimensional vs. 4-factor comparison as a first deliverable.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses whether single safety scores are psychometrically valid with a concrete MIRT approach on AIR-Bench; safety relevance is immediate.

ideas.title: CAT Transfer to Safety-Relevant Non-Knowledge Domains

original_idea.body:
# CAT Transfer to Safety-Relevant Non-Knowledge Domains

**Problem:** Medical CAT achieved r=0.988 with full-bank scores using only 1.3% of items (arXiv 2603.23506). But medical benchmarks are pure knowledge retrieval. Safety evaluation involves reasoning about edge cases, values alignment, and multi-step refusal logic — domains where ability may be multidimensional and item information functions may differ fundamentally from knowledge recall.

**Direction:** Using a public safety benchmark with item-level scores (e.g., AdvBench, TruthfulQA, or HELM safety tasks), calibrate a MIRT model in R (mirt package). Simulate CAT administration to 20–30 models and compare CAT-estimated ability scores to full-bank scores. Compute correlation and mean absolute error. Compare convergence curves (items needed) against the medical benchmark result.

**Why it matters:** If CAT efficiency does not transfer to safety domains, the efficiency gains exploited by adaptive testing are specific to knowledge domains and cannot be used to speed up safety evaluations.

**Relevant context:** arXiv 2603.23506 (medical CAT, r=0.988, 1.3% items); mirt CAT simulation (mirtCAT package in R); TruthfulQA, AdvBench public data; MIRT for multidimensional domains.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: determines whether adaptive testing can make safety evaluation more efficient. The answer (yes or no) informs evaluation strategy but does not directly reduce a specific catastrophic risk.

low_compute.reasoning: MIRT calibration and CAT simulation in R. No model inference needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires both MIRT modeling (advanced) and CAT simulation (mirtCAT package). The combination of multidimensional calibration with adaptive testing simulation is substantially complex. Understanding why MIRT vs. unidimensional IRT matters for CAT requires deep psychometric knowledge.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Could be scoped to unidimensional CAT on one benchmark as a first deliverable, but the stated direction requires MIRT which adds complexity. The comparison to medical benchmarks requires obtaining or reproducing that result.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses whether adaptive testing efficiency transfers to safety evaluation domains with a concrete MIRT-CAT simulation; safety relevance is immediate.

ideas.title: Cold Start and Capability Overhang: When New Architecture Meets Uncharted Capability Space

original_idea.body:
# Cold Start and Capability Overhang: When New Architecture Meets Uncharted Capability Space

**Problem:** The cold-start problem (Failure A10) means benchmarks are calibrated on existing model families and may not have valid difficulty parameters for genuinely novel architectures. Capability overhang (Failure B4) means novel architectures may have unexpected capability profiles. Together these create a double blind spot: we cannot know what a novel architecture's true capability ceiling is because our benchmarks are calibrated on different model families, and any apparent capability gap may be an artifact of miscalibrated items rather than genuine limitation.

**Direction:** Select 2–3 recently released architecturally novel models (e.g., MoE models, models with novel context architectures). Apply IRT analysis (mirt in R) using item calibrations derived from existing model families. Test whether item difficulties and discriminations transfer to the novel architecture by computing residuals between expected and observed response patterns (person-fit statistics). Identify items with large residuals — these are the items where the novel architecture is behaving unexpectedly relative to established ability curves. Interpret clusters of unexpected items as potential capability overhang indicators requiring deeper investigation.

**Why it matters:** IRT person-fit analysis on novel model families provides a principled, psychometrically grounded method for flagging capability patterns that do not fit established models — which is precisely the operationalization of 'capability overhang' detection. This is more principled than ad hoc inspection of score anomalies.

**Relevant context:** IRT calibration is population-specific; applying calibrations from one population to another is a known validity concern in psychometrics. Novel architectures (MoE, extended context) are actively deployed. Person-fit statistics available in mirt. Capability overhang is a documented safety concern.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: miscalibrated benchmarks may miss capability overhang in novel architectures. The risk mechanism is named but the chain has a gap: finding IRT misfit does not directly reduce overhang risk without a response protocol.

low_compute.reasoning: Uses existing benchmark data and R/mirt for IRT analysis. Light compute; all analysis is statistical on existing response matrices.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires understanding IRT calibration transfer, person-fit statistics, and interpreting residual patterns as capability overhang indicators. Advanced psychometric reasoning needed.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires selecting novel models, applying IRT with transferred calibrations, computing person-fit, and interpreting clusters. Multiple analytical steps, though the person-fit analysis for one model family could be a first deliverable.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses capability overhang detection for novel architectures using IRT person-fit analysis; safety relevance is immediate for evaluating new model families.

ideas.title: Item Exposure Control Analysis for AI Safety Benchmarks

original_idea.body:
# Item Exposure Control Analysis for AI Safety Benchmarks: Quantifying Data Leakage Risk Using Exposure Rate Diagnostics

**Problem:** AI safety benchmark items that are heavily exposed during training data collection inflate model performance beyond what genuine safety would predict—analogous to the CAT problem of overexposed items. There is no formal framework for quantifying which safety benchmark items are at highest contamination risk based on their characteristics.

**Direction:** Apply IRT-based item exposure analysis to AI safety benchmarks. Estimate item difficulty parameters using IRT. Identify items that are disproportionately 'overselected' by current models relative to their difficulty level—a pattern suggesting familiarity rather than safety generalization. Compare item difficulty-to-selection ratios against exposure rate thresholds used in CAT (e.g., Sympson-Hetter threshold of 0.5). Correlate exposure risk indicators with known data leakage signals (n-gram match with training corpora, semantic similarity to web-scraped safety datasets). Propose item rotation or item banking procedures analogous to CAT exposure control.

**Why it matters:** Item exposure control in CAT uses formal statistical methods to prevent test score inflation from item overexposure. AI benchmark contamination has been identified as a major threat to valid evaluation (Benchmark Contamination article). Applying formal exposure control diagnostics would provide a quantitative framework for contamination risk assessment that goes beyond simple n-gram matching. The methodology requires only IRT analysis and correlation in R.

**Relevant context:** IRT item exposure control literature is well-developed (Springer 2023, PMC6140306). AI benchmark contamination is documented and discussed as a major problem ('Benchmark Contamination: The AI Fraud Nobody Wants to Discuss'). N-gram overlap methods for contamination detection exist. The formal analogy between CAT item exposure and benchmark contamination is conceptually clear but appears not to have been developed in published work.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: contaminated items inflate safety scores, and exposure control identifies high-risk items. But the analogy between CAT exposure and benchmark contamination is loose; contamination in training is not the same as item overselection in adaptive testing.

low_compute.reasoning: IRT analysis in R plus correlation with n-gram overlap. Light compute; n-gram matching on benchmark items is not heavy.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires understanding both CAT exposure control theory and contamination detection methods, plus bridging two distinct frameworks. The conceptual bridge between CAT exposure and training contamination is novel and requires advanced reasoning.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Multiple components: IRT calibration, exposure rate computation, correlation with contamination signals, and proposing rotation procedures. The exposure rate analysis alone could be a first deliverable but the full analysis is sustained.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses contamination risk in safety benchmarks with concrete IRT exposure analysis methodology; safety relevance is immediate for benchmark integrity.

ideas.title: Are IRT Item Parameters Stable Across Prompt Phrasings? Testing Measurement Invariance

original_idea.body:
# Are IRT Item Parameters Stable Across Prompt Phrasings? Testing Measurement Invariance for Safety Items

**Problem:** Quantify and reduce prompt sensitivity in evaluation

**Direction:** For 20-30 safety items, create 3-4 paraphrase variants of each. Calibrate IRT item parameters (difficulty b, discrimination a) separately for each paraphrase group. Test whether parameters are stable across phrasings using IRT measurement invariance tests (multigroup IRT in mirt, testing equality constraints on a and b parameters). Items with significantly different parameters across phrasings are 'prompt-sensitive' in a psychometrically precise sense.

**Why it matters:** If an item's IRT parameters change depending on how it is phrased, then the item is not measuring a stable construct—different phrasings are effectively measuring different things. This makes it impossible to compare model ability estimates across evaluations that use different prompt wordings. Identifying prompt-stable items is essential for benchmark validity.

**Relevant context:** IRT measurement invariance testing (multigroup IRT, differential item functioning frameworks) is a well-established psychometric technique. 'Diagnosing the Reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge via Item Response Theory' (2025) applies IRT to judge reliability—similar methods apply to prompt stability. The mirt package supports multigroup IRT and measurement invariance testing.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: prompt-sensitive items undermine benchmark validity, making safety claims unreliable across evaluation settings. The risk mechanism is named but the impact requires adoption of prompt-stable items by benchmark developers.

low_compute.reasoning: Requires running 2-3 models across 3-4 paraphrase variants of 20-30 items (180-360 API calls). Moderate cost for data collection, though analysis is light.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires creating paraphrase variants, running multigroup IRT, and testing measurement invariance constraints. Multigroup IRT with equality constraints is advanced psychometric methodology.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires creating paraphrases, collecting responses, calibrating IRT per group, and testing invariance. Multiple sequential steps, though the invariance test on a small item set could be focused.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses prompt sensitivity in safety evaluation using multigroup IRT measurement invariance; safety relevance is immediate for evaluation validity.

ideas.title: Prompt-Robust Safety Scoring: Aggregating Across Paraphrases Using IRT Theta Estimates

original_idea.body:
# Prompt-Robust Safety Scoring: Aggregating Across Paraphrases Using IRT Theta Estimates

**Problem:** Quantify and reduce prompt sensitivity in evaluation

**Direction:** Compare three scoring methods for safety evaluation: (1) mean proportion of refusals across all prompts (raw score), (2) IRT theta estimate from a calibrated model using all prompt variants, (3) IRT theta estimate using only prompt-stable items (those with invariant parameters). Assess which scoring method produces the most stable model rankings across held-out prompt sets. Use rank correlation stability as the primary outcome.

**Why it matters:** IRT theta estimation accounts for item difficulty and discrimination, potentially producing more stable ability estimates than raw refusal rates. If IRT-based scoring is more robust to prompt variation than raw scoring, this provides a concrete, practical recommendation for how safety benchmark scores should be reported.

**Relevant context:** tinyBenchmarks (2024) showed that IRT-based estimates outperform raw scores on general capability benchmarks. 'Adaptive Testing for LLM Evaluation' (2025) demonstrates the superiority of IRT theta over raw scores for stability. The extension to safety-specific benchmarks with prompt-robust scoring has not been investigated.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: prompt-sensitive scoring makes safety claims unreliable, and IRT-based scoring may be more robust. The chain names the mechanism but impact depends on whether IRT scoring is actually adopted by benchmark developers.

low_compute.reasoning: Requires collecting model responses across multiple prompt variants for multiple models. Moderate API cost for data collection.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires understanding three different scoring methods, IRT theta estimation, measurement invariance for item selection, and rank correlation analysis across held-out sets. Multiple advanced techniques needed.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Depends on prior work (calibrated IRT parameters, prompt-stable item identification). The scoring comparison itself is focused but has upstream dependencies.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses prompt sensitivity with concrete IRT-based robust scoring methodology; safety relevance is clear for reliable safety measurement.

ideas.title: Exploratory Factor Analysis of AI Safety Benchmarks

original_idea.body:
# Exploratory Factor Analysis of AI Safety Benchmarks: Discovering the Latent Structure of Safety

**Problem:** P1: No IRT applied to AI safety benchmarks

**Direction:** Apply EFA to a matrix of model scores across multiple safety benchmark subscales, discovering the latent factor structure of 'AI safety' and testing whether a single safety dimension or multiple orthogonal safety dimensions best account for observed benchmark intercorrelations.

**Why it matters:** The dimensionality of 'safety' is empirically unknown—current benchmarks assume it is either unidimensional (single score) or fully multidimensional (independent subscales). EFA would provide the first data-driven answer to this question, directly informing whether IRT (which assumes unidimensionality) or MIRT is the appropriate framework.

**Relevant context:** EFA is a standard tool in the psychometrician's toolkit. The 'General Scales' paper (arxiv 2503.06378) applies similar factor analysis to general capabilities. Applying EFA to safety-specific benchmark subscores (harmlessness, truthfulness, jailbreak, privacy, etc.) across a set of models is a novel analysis feasible with public leaderboard data and R (psych package).

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: EFA reveals whether safety benchmarks measure distinct constructs or a general factor, which matters for understanding what benchmarks actually test. Gap is in connecting factor structure findings to specific catastrophic risk reduction.

low_compute.reasoning: Factor analysis on existing response matrices. CPU-only, standard packages.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: EFA requires understanding of factor extraction, rotation methods, and interpretation. Intermediate statistics knowledge needed but methodology is well-documented.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Deliverable requires collecting multi-benchmark response data, choosing extraction/rotation methods, and interpreting factor structure — sustained effort but concrete.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses the unknown dimensionality of safety constructs with EFA, informing whether IRT or MIRT is appropriate for safety evaluation.

ideas.title: Test Equating Safety Benchmarks: Putting TruthfulQA and WildGuard on a Common Scale

original_idea.body:
# Test Equating Safety Benchmarks: Putting TruthfulQA and WildGuard on a Common Scale

**Problem:** Different safety benchmarks (TruthfulQA, WildGuard, HarmBench, StereoSet) produce scores on incomparable scales, making it impossible to say a model is 'safer overall'. IRT-based test equating can place multiple benchmarks on a common theta scale using anchor items (items appearing in multiple benchmarks) or concurrent calibration.

**Direction:** Identify items or item types that appear in two or more safety benchmarks (or create a small set of anchor items scored on multiple benchmarks for a set of models). Use IRT concurrent calibration (mirt R package) or fixed-parameter linking to place at least two safety benchmarks on a common latent scale. Compute linked safety ability estimates for 30+ models. Compare rankings before and after equating. Assess equating precision using the standard error of equating.

**Why it matters:** A common safety scale would allow meaningful aggregation across benchmarks and a defensible overall safety ranking. This is the measurement foundation for any future 'safety index' or composite safety score. Test equating is standard practice in educational assessment but has never been applied across AI safety benchmarks.

**Relevant context:** Test equating fundamentals (cogn-iq.org 2025 summary); IRT equating via concurrent calibration; Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.0 combines multiple benchmarks but without formal equating; metabench and tinyBenchmarks work toward common benchmarking but without explicit IRT equating.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: a common safety scale enables meaningful cross-benchmark comparison, which improves regulatory decisions. The specific gap is that equating two benchmarks is a proof of concept -- practical adoption requires broader buy-in.

low_compute.reasoning: IRT calibration in R on existing data. No model inference required.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Test equating is an advanced psychometric topic. Concurrent calibration, fixed-parameter linking, and equating precision assessment require specialized knowledge beyond basic IRT. Finding or creating anchor items is itself a non-trivial research challenge.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Could focus on equating just two benchmarks using models tested on both as virtual anchors. That is reasonably scoped, but the anchor identification step and equating validation require sustained effort.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses cross-benchmark comparability for safety evaluation with a concrete IRT equating methodology; safety relevance is immediate for aggregating safety evidence.

ideas.title: IRT-Based Equipercentile Equating to Compare Models Across Different Safety Benchmarks

original_idea.body:
# IRT-Based Equipercentile Equating to Compare Models Across Different Safety Benchmarks

**Problem:** GPT-4o is evaluated on HarmBench while Gemini Ultra is evaluated on WildGuard. Their scores cannot be directly compared because the benchmarks differ in difficulty, item type, and construct coverage. The field has no principled way to put scores from different safety evaluations on a common scale.

**Direction:** Apply IRT-based equating: calibrate item parameters for both benchmarks on a shared set of 'anchor items' (common items or a common sample of models), then transform scores onto a single latent scale. Alternatively, use equipercentile equating if IRT assumptions are not met. Use the Open LLM Leaderboard data where multiple models have been tested on multiple benchmarks, identify overlapping models as a 'virtual anchor group,' and produce linked scores. Report model rankings before and after equating to show divergences. Implement in R (equate package).

**Why it matters:** Cross-benchmark equating is prerequisite for any meta-analysis of AI safety, for regulatory comparisons across labs, and for tracking safety progress over time as benchmarks are updated. The psychometric equating literature has 70 years of theory directly applicable to this problem.

**Relevant context:** IRT equating literature shows separate calibration procedures outperform concurrent calibration. arXiv 2505.15055 and Stanford CRFM work already fit IRT models to LLM benchmark data. The equate R package implements equipercentile and IRT-based equating. Open LLM Leaderboard provides multi-benchmark multi-model data publicly.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: cross-benchmark equating enables meaningful comparison across labs and regulatory contexts. The mechanism is well-defined but the chain to catastrophic risk reduction is indirect -- it improves measurement infrastructure.

low_compute.reasoning: IRT equating in R on existing leaderboard data. No model inference needed.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Test equating is an advanced psychometric specialty. Identifying virtual anchor groups, performing IRT-based or equipercentile equating, and assessing equating precision requires specialized knowledge. The equate package helps but understanding the methodology is challenging.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Could be scoped to equipercentile equating of two benchmarks using overlapping models, which is simpler than full IRT equating. But even the minimal version requires careful anchor identification and validation.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses cross-benchmark comparability for safety evaluation with a concrete IRT equating methodology; safety relevance is clear for regulatory comparisons.

ideas.title: Measurement Invariance Testing of Safety Evaluations Across Language/Cultural Contexts

original_idea.body:
# Measurement Invariance Testing of Safety Evaluations Across Language/Cultural Contexts

**Problem:** Safety evaluations are predominantly developed and validated in English. When applied across languages and cultural contexts, the assumption of measurement invariance — that items function the same way across groups — may be violated. A model might appear safe in English evaluation but deploy unsafely in Spanish or Arabic contexts, because the evaluation items did not travel. This is a DIF problem at the language/culture level.

**Direction:** Using a multilingual safety benchmark (e.g., if multilingual versions of safety items exist) or by translating a subset of safety items from a standard English benchmark into 2-3 other languages (using professional translation + back-translation verification), administer items across language conditions. Fit multigroup IRT models in R (mirt supports multigroup analysis), testing for configural, metric, and scalar invariance. Items showing differential item functioning across language groups (DIF) are flagged as culturally non-invariant. Quantify the impact of non-invariant items on overall score comparability across language groups. Identify item content features (legal references, cultural norms, specific harm scenarios) that predict invariance failure.

**Why it matters:** Models deployed globally are evaluated in English but cause harm in multilingual contexts. Measurement non-invariance across languages means that a single global safety score is an invalid composite — it may reflect English-context safety while obscuring cross-lingual vulnerabilities.

**Relevant context:** Cross-lingual contamination was identified as a benchmark validity issue (2025). Measurement invariance testing is standard in cross-cultural psychometrics. The mirt R package supports multigroup IRT for invariance testing. Translation + DIF analysis requires no ML, only psychometric expertise and translation resources. No prior paper has applied formal measurement invariance testing to AI safety benchmarks.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: English-only safety evaluation -> non-invariant items mask cross-lingual vulnerabilities -> models deploy unsafely in non-English contexts. Every link is explicit and targets a real deployment risk for globally deployed models.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based IRT analysis is CPU-only, but administering items to models across languages requires API calls, which have modest cost. Translation also requires resources.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Multigroup IRT with configural/metric/scalar invariance testing is advanced psychometric methodology. Additionally, professional translation with back-translation verification adds logistical complexity. This requires specialized knowledge well beyond beginner ML skills.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires translation of items, multilingual benchmark administration, multigroup IRT fitting, and DIF analysis. Multiple languages multiply the effort. No clear self-contained first deliverable that avoids the translation logistics.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses cross-lingual safety evaluation validity with concrete multigroup IRT methodology; safety relevance is immediate for global AI deployment.

ideas.title: IRT-Based Score Equating Between Safety Benchmarks: A Linking Study

original_idea.body:
# IRT-Based Score Equating Between Safety Benchmarks: A Linking Study

**Problem:** A model evaluated on SafetyBench cannot be compared to one evaluated on HarmBench — the scales are incommensurable. Labs choose whichever benchmark makes their model look best. There are no IRT-based equating or linking studies for safety benchmarks, so cross-benchmark comparisons are scientifically indefensible.

**Direction:** Identify a set of 'anchor items' — safety prompts that appear in conceptually equivalent form across two safety benchmarks (e.g., SafetyBench and TrustLLM, or HarmBench and WildGuard). Evaluate a common set of 15-25 models on both benchmarks. Use the equateIRT R package to perform concurrent IRT calibration or common-person linking. Place both benchmarks on a common latent scale. Compute equating error. Assess whether scores from the two benchmarks can be meaningfully compared.

**Why it matters:** Fills the equating gap in Success State 3. Without equating, the field cannot aggregate evidence across evaluations or track safety progress across benchmark generations. This is a prerequisite for any meta-analytic or regulatory synthesis of safety evidence.

**Relevant context:** The equateIRT R package (CRAN, updated July 2025) provides all necessary tools. Common-persons design (Liu et al., 2026) shows that 30+ common persons suffice for equating. IRT parameter stability under equating conditions (Frontiers, 2025) provides methodological guidance. No AI safety benchmark equating study exists in the literature.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: incommensurable benchmark scales -> labs cherry-pick favorable benchmarks -> inconsistent safety standards. Equating enables cross-benchmark comparison. But the link to reducing catastrophic risk has a gap; comparability is a prerequisite for better governance but does not directly prevent harm.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based equating analysis is CPU-only, but evaluating 15-25 models on two benchmarks via API requires moderate API costs if data is not already available.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: IRT equating (concurrent calibration, common-person linking, equating error) is advanced psychometric methodology. Identifying valid anchor items across benchmarks requires expert judgment. This is graduate-level psychometric work, not accessible to beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires anchor item identification, dual-benchmark evaluation of many models, and equating analysis. Multiple data collection and analysis steps with dependencies. Not a single focused experiment.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses cross-benchmark comparability for safety evaluation with concrete IRT equating; safety relevance is immediate for regulatory synthesis.

ideas.title: Measurement Invariance Testing: Do Safety Benchmarks Measure the Same Construct Across Model Families?

original_idea.body:
# Measurement Invariance Testing: Do Safety Benchmarks Measure the Same Construct Across Model Families?

**Problem:** Safety evaluations are used to compare models across different architectural families (GPT-style, Claude-style, Gemini-style, open-source). But if a safety benchmark measures different latent constructs for different model families — measurement non-invariance — cross-family comparisons are invalid. This has never been tested.

**Direction:** Using multi-group CFA (in lavaan), test configural, metric, and scalar invariance of a safety benchmark across model families (e.g., GPT-4 class vs. Claude class vs. open-source LLaMA class). Collect item-level response data for models grouped by family. Test whether factor loadings and item intercepts are equal across groups. Report which levels of invariance hold. Identify non-invariant items. Discuss implications for cross-family safety comparisons.

**Why it matters:** Fills a measurement fairness gap overlapping Success States 2 and 3. If items are non-invariant across model families, then 'GPT-4 scores 82% vs. Claude scores 79%' on a safety benchmark is not a valid comparison — the benchmark means different things for different architectures. This finding would have immediate practical implications for evaluation policy.

**Relevant context:** Measurement invariance is a standard CFA extension implemented in lavaan. The 'Measuring what Matters' review did not address measurement invariance across model families. # Multidimensional IRT (MIRT) for Safety Capability Profiles

**Problem:** Unidimensional IRT places all models on a single safety axis, but safety is plausibly multidimensional: a model may be highly calibrated at refusing harmful requests in English but poor at detecting harm in multilingual or low-resource language contexts. MIRT can recover multiple latent dimensions simultaneously but has not been applied to safety evaluation.

**Direction:** Fit a 2-factor or 3-factor MIRT model to item-level safety benchmark response data using the mirt R package. Use exploratory MIRT to let the data reveal the latent structure, then confirmatory MIRT to test theoretically motivated structures. Examine factor loadings to interpret dimensions. Compute model-specific theta vectors (safety profiles). Visualize models in 2D/3D theta space. Identify whether multilingual, reasoning-intensive, and refusal-type items load on distinct factors.

**Why it matters:** Addresses Success State 7. MIRT provides richer diagnostic information than unidimensional IRT without requiring the discrete attribute assumptions of CDMs. Combined with CDM work, this triangulates whether AI safety is best modeled as continuous multidimensional traits or discrete attribute mastery.

**Relevant context:** The mirt R package (Chalmers, GitHub) is the standard tool and well-documented. A 2024 paper on MIRT for competency assessment (ScienceDirect) and a 2025 paper on human vs. AI-generated test dimensionality (arxiv 2510.24739) provide methodological grounding. MIRT for LLM ability profiling is nascent — no safety application exists.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: unidimensional safety scores mask multidimensional vulnerabilities -> MIRT reveals distinct safety dimensions -> enables targeted interventions. The chain names the risk mechanism (masked vulnerabilities) but the gap is that revealing dimensions does not directly reduce risk without downstream action.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based MIRT analysis using the mirt package. CPU-only, no model training.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Exploratory and confirmatory MIRT, factor rotation, bifactor modeling, and factor loading interpretation require advanced psychometric expertise. This is graduate-level methodology not accessible to CS beginners even with mentoring.

narrow_scope.reasoning: The deliverable (factor structure + theta profiles) is clear, but exploratory-then-confirmatory MIRT is a multi-step analytical pipeline requiring careful model comparison and interpretation. Not a single focused experiment.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses multidimensional safety profiling with concrete MIRT methodology; safety relevance is immediate for revealing domain-specific vulnerabilities.

ideas.title: General Factor (g-factor) Analysis of AI Safety: Is There a Single Safety Latent Trait?

original_idea.body:
# General Factor (g-factor) Analysis of AI Safety: Is There a Single Safety Latent Trait?

**Problem:** The field implicitly debates whether AI safety is a single latent trait (a 'g-factor' of safety) or a collection of independent capabilities. This has profound implications: if a g-factor exists, a short unidimensional IRT scale is sufficient; if safety is multidimensional, a single score is misleading. No empirical test of this question exists.

**Direction:** Collect item-level or subdomain-level safety benchmark scores across 5-7 diverse safety benchmarks for a common set of models. Run exploratory factor analysis (EFA) with different rotation methods (varimax, oblimin). Test for a general factor using bi-factor modeling (bifactor function in mirt). Compute omega-hierarchical and omega-total to quantify how much variance is attributable to the general safety factor vs. specific subdomain factors. Report whether a single safety score is a defensible summary statistic.

**Why it matters:** Foundational for all of Success States 1-7. If a g-factor of safety exists and accounts for >70% of variance, the entire field can focus on measuring it well (IRT, reliability, standard setting) rather than chasing subdomains. If safety is truly multidimensional, single scores are misleading and the entire benchmark paradigm needs restructuring.

**Relevant context:** Bi-factor modeling is natively supported in mirt. Omega statistics are computed in the psych R package. EFA of safety constructs is implied by the nomological network work but not executed. The 'General Scales Unlock AI Evaluation' paper (arxiv 2503.06378) discusses general scales for AI evaluation but focuses on prediction rather than psychometric structure.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: if safety is multidimensional, single scores mask domain-specific vulnerabilities -> g-factor analysis determines the correct measurement paradigm -> directly informs whether the entire benchmark ecosystem needs restructuring. High-leverage foundational question with cascading implications.

low_compute.reasoning: R-based EFA and bifactor modeling using mirt and psych packages. CPU-only.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Bifactor modeling, EFA with multiple rotations, omega-hierarchical computation, and g-factor interpretation require advanced psychometric training. This is graduate-level methodology not accessible to CS students with beginner ML skills.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Requires collecting data across 5-7 diverse safety benchmarks for a common model set. The data assembly effort is substantial, and the multi-benchmark analytical pipeline has many steps. Not a self-contained single experiment.

original_idea.body:
# Graded Response Model for Partial Safety Credit: Beyond Binary Pass/Fail

**Problem:** Most safety benchmarks treat model responses as binary (safe/unsafe), discarding information about severity of harm or degree of refusal. A Graded Response Model (GRM) can model ordered polytomous responses (no harm, mild harm, severe harm; or full refusal, partial refusal, full compliance) and recover richer ability estimates. GRMs have never been applied to AI safety scoring.

**Direction:** Reannotate a subset of an existing safety dataset (e.g., 200-300 items from HarmBench or WildGuard) with a 3-4 level ordinal safety rubric (complete safe response, borderline, partial harm, severe harm) using human or LLM-as-judge ratings. Fit a GRM in R (mirt or ltm) to the polytomous responses across 30+ models. Compare model ability estimates from GRM against binary IRT estimates and against original benchmark scores. Report item characteristic curves for key safety items.

**Why it matters:** Binary pass/fail scoring throws away information about the magnitude of safety failures. A GRM provides more precise model ability estimates and reveals the probability of each harm level as a function of model safety ability. This is directly useful for regulatory thresholds: distinguishing 'occasionally mildly harmful' from 'rarely severely harmful' models.

**Relevant context:** Graded Response Model literature (Samejima); LLM-as-judge rubric-based scoring is now mainstream (Promptfoo, 2025); mirt R package supports GRM; WildGuard and HarmBench have published response data; partial credit in AI evaluation is a documented gap.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: richer scoring enables better regulatory thresholds, which improves deployment decisions. The specific risk mechanism (binary scoring loses severity information) is named, but the chain to reducing catastrophic risk has a gap -- better measurement precision is valuable but indirect.

low_compute.reasoning: Mostly R-based statistical modeling. The reannotation step using LLM-as-judge requires some API calls but is modest (200-300 items x 30 models).

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires both data reannotation (designing an ordinal rubric, running LLM-as-judge) and advanced psychometric modeling (GRM in mirt). The reannotation alone is a non-trivial research design task. GRM interpretation requires psychometric training.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Two distinct phases required: (1) reannotate 200-300 items with ordinal rubric across 30+ models, (2) fit and compare GRM vs binary IRT. The reannotation step alone is substantial and must be completed before any modeling can begin.

ideas.quick_reasoning: Directly addresses a recognized AI safety evaluation problem (binary scoring discards severity information) with a concrete GRM approach and clear safety implications for regulatory thresholds.

# Measurement Uncertainty Budget for IRT-Based Safety Scores: Quantifying Total Score Uncertainty

**Problem:** P1: No IRT applied to AI safety benchmarks

**Direction:** Apply GUM-style uncertainty budgeting to IRT-estimated safety ability scores, quantifying uncertainty from item calibration error, model response sampling, prompt variability, and ability estimation precision, producing a principled confidence interval for each model's IRT safety score.

**Relevant context:** GUM uncertainty budgeting is standard in physical measurement but novel for IRT-based AI scores. # Reliability Generalization Meta-Analysis of AI Safety Benchmark Internal Consistency

**Problem:** Reliability generalization (RG) meta-analysis examines how reliability varies across administrations of the same instrument. No RG meta-analysis has ever been conducted on AI safety benchmarks to ask: is a safety benchmark's internal consistency stable across different model samples, or does reliability fluctuate dramatically depending on which models are tested?

**Direction:** Collect internal consistency estimates (KR-20, split-half, or IRT-based marginal reliability) for 8-10 safety benchmarks across multiple published evaluation studies or leaderboard snapshots using different model pools. Compute reliability estimates for each benchmark-sample combination in R. Conduct a meta-regression predicting reliability from moderators: number of items, model pool diversity (range of scores), benchmark age, item format. Summarize using forest plots and report practical implications for benchmark design.

**Why it matters:** If safety benchmark reliability varies by 0.3 units across different model samples, safety rankings derived from those benchmarks are untrustworthy for specific populations of models. RG meta-analysis would reveal which safety benchmarks have robust, sample-independent reliability and which do not—providing the first systematic reliability evidence for the AI safety evaluation toolbox.

**Relevant context:** RG meta-analysis methodology (Springer 2023); Cronbach's alpha debate (EPR 2025); IRT marginal reliability is preferable to Cronbach's alpha for non-tau-equivalent items; reliability of AI benchmarks is an acknowledged gap (Stanford 2025 report on benchmark bugs).

# Interlaboratory Comparison Design for AI Safety Evaluation Reproducibility

**Problem:** Different labs evaluating the same model on the same benchmark obtain different scores due to implementation variation (prompt formatting, temperature, few-shot examples, evaluation harness). There is no formal system for quantifying this inter-lab variability, analogous to the interlaboratory comparison (ILC) programs used in analytical chemistry and clinical testing.

**Direction:** Design and run a mini-ILC study: recruit 4–6 teams (academic labs, independent researchers) to independently evaluate the same 10 models on the same 3 safety benchmarks, using their own implementation choices but the same item set. Use ISO 13528 statistical methods (z-scores, En numbers) to identify outlier labs and quantify reproducibility (between-lab standard deviation). Identify which benchmarks are most and least reproducible. Report uncertainty estimates analogous to a measurement uncertainty budget.

**Why it matters:** ILC programs are the cornerstone of measurement quality assurance in every physical and chemical measurement field. An analogous program for AI safety benchmarks would reveal how much of reported score variation is real model differences vs. implementation noise—directly impacting how seriously benchmarks should be taken in governance decisions.

**Relevant context:** ISO 13528:2022 provides the statistical framework for ILC data analysis. The benchmark-iceberg phenomenon (OpenReview, IRT-iceberg paper) shows hidden implementation choices dominate score variance. Mini-ILC can be run with volunteer collaboration. Analysis is entirely in R. Directly actionable for safety governance.
